idiom_name: trait Updatable with Vec<Box<dyn Updatable>> walked by for
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so the hook is a trait (trait Updatable { fn update(&mut self, dt: f32); }) and the collection is a Vec of trait objects or a &mut [dyn Updatable] slice, walked by a for loop. What replaces the classic structure: trait plus impl replaces the class hierarchy and the Vec replaces the entity manager, while &mut enforces at compile time that exactly one step mutates an entity at a time. The dynamic-dispatch form is the right default when the kind set is open; for a closed set an enum plus match gives static dispatch and no per-entity allocation, and Bevy's Update schedule is the engine-level form where the walk itself disappears into the scheduler.
pitfalls: Trait objects are dynamically sized and need indirection: Vec<Box<dyn Trait>> allocates per entity and chases pointers, while Vec<&mut dyn Trait> or an enum avoids the allocation.

The borrow checker forbids restructuring the collection while stepping (a step cannot spawn or remove through &mut self): collect commands during the walk and apply them afterwards, or pass a command buffer.
Object safety: generic methods or associated constants make a trait unusable as dyn, so keep the hook signature object-safe.
f32 dt accumulates drift over long sessions; keep the cadence in a duration/accumulator and pass dt as f32 only at the boundary.

variants.name: Bevy Update schedule with systems over queries
variants.implementation_notes: Bevy inverts the pattern: instead of objects with update methods, each per-frame step is a system registered in the Update schedule - docs.rs: 'The schedule that contains any app logic that must run once per render frame. For most gameplay logic, consider using FixedUpdate instead' - and systems query the components they act on, with explicit ordering constraints. What replaces the classic structure: the ECS world replaces the entity collection and the scheduler replaces the driver, so there is no per-object dispatch at all - behaviour lives in systems, data in components, which is the data-oriented answer to the pattern's locality caveat. Choose it when the project is a Bevy game; the dyn-trait variant stays the right shape for std-only Rust.
pitfalls: Gameplay that must be deterministic belongs in FixedUpdate, not Update ('For most gameplay logic, consider using FixedUpdate instead').
System order is not source order: without .chain()/.before()/.after() constraints, two systems touching the same component are ambiguous and Bevy rejects conflicting access.
Systems run in parallel when their data access allows it, so a step may execute on another thread: Send + Sync bounds and deferred Commands replace the single-threaded walk.

Structural changes (spawn/despawn) go through Commands and apply at the next schedule point, so entities created this frame do not act until the next frame - a feature that surprises ports of OO update lists.
